extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, administrative law practitioners, federal agency lawyers, and policymakers concerned with First Amendment issues on agency social media
extracted.subtask_short: agency social media First Amendment analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether speech on federal agency social media is government speech, private speech in a public forum, or mixed speech, and applying doctrinal tests and practical factors to decide which First Amendment framework governs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Johanns two-prong government-speech test (message and control)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the government can prove that it developed a message and exercised control over the communication of that message, it has satisfied the two prongs of government speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorship need not be literal government authorship — a private third party may develop the message so long as a government official maintains veto power. Effective control over content and dissemination is critical. Courts look for an identifiable established message and the government's ability to approve or disapprove specific communications. Evidence of control can include program oversight, appointment authority, and power of the purse. The government need not reveal itself as author; the Court has treated elections and political accountability as a mechanism for oversight (though that assumption has been criticized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public forum doctrine applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: When speech is that of private individuals on government property (or in a forum the government has opened to private speakers), courts apply the public forum doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public forum regime governs private expression in spaces the government has opened for public discourse. The public forum doctrine has been criticized as ill-suited in some institutional contexts, but remains the operative framework when the site functions as a place for private speakers rather than as the government's own message vehicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed (hybrid) speech identification (spectrum approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some contexts produce 'mixed' or 'hybrid' speech that contains both private and governmental components; speech should be viewed on a spectrum from private to government with classification depending on which component predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include government employees' speech, advertisements on public transit, specialty license plates, artistic expression funded by government grants, and federal agency social media that both promotes agency activities and provides a forum for private speakers. Because Supreme Court doctrine treats categories as mutually exclusive, agencies must decide where their social media lands on the continuum; the predominating type of speech drives the doctrinal choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Johanns/common factors for attributing speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have asked: who is the literal speaker, who exercises editorial control, what is the purpose of the program, and who bears ultimate responsibility?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors (literal speaker, editorial control, program purpose, ultimate responsibility) were used by appellate courts before Johanns and remain relevant in assessing government versus private speech. Different circuits may emphasize different elements (e.g., editorial control in the Sixth Circuit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Page (Fourth Circuit) indicators of government control over a website
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding that a website is government speech can rest on evidence that the site has an established message and that the government retains effective control over links and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fourth Circuit identified five specific factors supporting control: (1) the government selected links that supported its own message; (2) the government maintained control over its website and could exclude links at any time; (3) the government did not incorporate information from linked sites onto its own site; (4) the government continuously communicated its position and buttressed it by referencing supporters; and (5) a disclaimer indicated that only the speech on the website was the government's. The court noted interactive features (chat rooms, message boards) could change the analysis toward a limited public forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government enterprise / curator-selection contexts may qualify as government speech
rubrics_metrics.description: When government performs institutional roles (broadcaster, patron of the arts, librarian, museum curator), its selective choices in performing those roles may constitute government speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Forbes, NEA v. Finley, and American Library Ass'n show that selectivity inherent to institutional decisionmaking (e.g., selecting art for an exhibit, programming public broadcasting, curating collections) can be treated as government expression. Courts analogize selection of private messages (books, artworks, monuments) to government speech in these contexts; but commentators debate whether institutional necessities should permit viewpoint discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rust / funding-program distinction (funding decision vs viewpoint discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restricting speech within a government-funded program can be treated as a funding decision rather than impermissible viewpoint discrimination if the program promotes the government's own message rather than facilitating private speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Rust v. Sullivan, the Court treated restrictions on speech by government-funded doctors (regarding abortion counseling) as funding decisions. Legal Services Corp. v. Velazquez later explained that Rust relied on government-speech reasoning: if a program is designed to facilitate private speech (not to promote a governmental message), content-based restrictions may violate the First Amendment. Thus, whether a subsidy or program's purpose is to promote government expression or to create a forum for private expression matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and practical risks of choosing a doctrine for agency social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies face tradeoffs: treating social-media spaces as public forums or as government speech each creates legal and practical risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency treats a site as a public forum and permits offensive, hate, or false speech, it may appear to endorse that speech and could face civil liability (e.g., contributory negligence) or reputational harm. If an agency treats the site as government speech and removes or refuses to post comments, it risks being found to violate the First Amendment if courts deem the comments protected private speech; adverse publicity and resource drains are additional considerations. Given these stakes, agencies should carefully assess which doctrine best fits their interactive platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet/social media characteristics relevant to forum analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet (and Web 2.0 interactive platforms) presents unique features—chat rooms, blogs, wikis, social networking pages—that affect forum analysis but have not been definitively classified by the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reno emphasized the Internet as 'vast democratic forums' and likened chat rooms to town criers, but the Court declined to set the level of First Amendment scrutiny for the medium. Lower courts have applied both doctrines to websites with limited guidance. The interactive qualities of social media (ability for the public to post/comment) are crucial: basic informational websites with no public discourse are more likely to be government speech; interactive comment-enabled platforms may be treated as limited public fora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary markers of effective control (examples cited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific manifestations of governmental control that courts have relied upon include appointment/oversight power, veto authority over content, continuous message communication, and disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johanns and subsequent cases treat factors such as the Secretary or agency overseeing a program, appointment of officials, retention of veto power over content, and Congress's oversight/power of the purse as indicia that the government 'developed' and 'controlled' the message. Conversely, absence of such formal controls (but with final approval authority) may still suffice for some courts to find government speech, though commentators warn this can obscure viewpoint-discrimination concerns.
